summary: This is a Wikipedia article excerpt on LGBT rights in Hong Kong, a special administrative region of China, covering legal history, recognition of same-sex relationships, and related court cases. It traces decriminalisation of male homosexuality in 1991, the unequal age of consent and its court challenges, and a series of rulings on spousal visas, spousal tax and benefits, and civil partnerships. The excerpt ends mid-sentence in its discussion of a 2019 ruling against a civil partnerships challenge, and the page notes the government has no plans to legalise same-sex marriage.
one_line: Overview of Hong Kong's legal history on LGBT rights, including decriminalisation, age of consent, same-sex visas, benefits and marriage litigation.
key_facts: In 1991 the Legislative Council of Hong Kong agreed to decriminalise private, adult, non-commercial, and consensual homosexual relations.
The age of consent was unequal, set at 21 for gay men and 16 for heterosexuals, and the law was silent about lesbianism.
In 2005 Justice Hartmann found the unequal age of consent unconstitutional under the Bill of Rights Ordinance, a ruling upheld by the Court of Appeal.
The provisions on unequal age of consent were not formally removed from the Crimes Ordinance (Cap. 200) until 2014.
On 30 May 2019 the High Court in Yeung Chu Wing v Secretary for Justice struck down four further provisions that imposed higher penalties for offences committed by homosexual men.
In June 2009 the Hong Kong Government extended limited recognition and protection to cohabitating same-sex couples under the Domestic Violence Ordinance.

In 2013 Hong Kong's High Court ruled that a transgender woman can marry her boyfriend and gave the government one year to draft a law for post-operation transsexual or transgender individuals to marry.
On 25 September 2017 the Court of Appeal ruled in favour of a British woman known as QT, finding her same-sex spouse should be granted a spousal visa.
On 4 July 2018 the Court of Final Appeal, led by Chief Justice Geoffrey Ma Tao-li, mandated that same-sex partners be granted spousal visas previously available only to heterosexual couples.

The spousal visa ruling became effective on 19 September 2018, when the Director of Immigration announced it would favourably consider same-sex civil partnership and marriage applications made outside Hong Kong.
On 28 April 2017 the Hong Kong High Court ruled in favour of Angus Leung Chun-kwong, calling the Civil Service Bureau's policy indirect discrimination.

On 6 June 2019 the Court of Final Appeal reversed the Court of Appeal's 2018 ruling, holding that the Civil Service Bureau and Inland Revenue Department had unlawfully discriminated against Leung and Scott Adams.
In July 2018 Chief Executive Carrie Lam said the government had no plans to amend the law to approve same-sex marriage in the near future.
In October 2019 the Court of First Instance ruled against MK, upholding the existing marriage law and continuing to deny civil partnerships to same-sex couples.
British nationals, including British Nationals (Overseas), can register civil partnerships with British consulates or embassies in 22 countries, but not in Hong Kong.

entities.name: Legislative Council of Hong Kong
entities.role: Body that agreed in 1991 to decriminalise private consensual homosexual relations and that LGBT groups lobbied on the age of consent

entities.name: Murray MacLehose
entities.role: Governor who privately supported gay rights but felt the local community would not support decriminalisation

entities.name: Justice Hartmann
entities.role: Judge who in 2005 found the unequal age of consent unconstitutional

entities.name: Yeung Chu-wing
entities.role: LGBT activist who brought the 2017 lawsuit that led to the 2019 High Court ruling striking down provisions under the Crimes Ordinance

entities.name: Andrew Cheung
entities.role: Chief judge who wrote in the 2017 Court of Appeal ruling that times have changed

entities.name: Geoffrey Ma Tao-li
entities.role: Chief Justice of the Court of Final Appeal who led the panel that ruled on spousal visas in 2018

entities.name: Carrie Lam
entities.role: Chief Executive of Hong Kong who said in 2018 the government had no plans to approve same-sex marriage

entities.name: Angus Leung Chun-kwong
entities.role: Hong Kong immigration officer who challenged the refusal to extend spousal benefits to his same-sex partner

entities.name: Scott Adams
entities.role: Same-sex partner of Angus Leung Chun-kwong, whom he married in New Zealand in 2014

entities.name: Anderson Chow Ka-ming
entities.role: High Court judge who ruled in Leung's favour in 2017 and later ruled against MK in 2019

entities.name: Ricky Chu Man-kin
entities.role: Equal Opportunities Commission chairman who preferred a step-by-step approach starting with anti-discrimination initiatives

entities.name: Stewart Wong
entities.role: Government lawyer who defended the existing marriage law in the civil partnerships hearings

entities.name: Dinah Rose QC
entities.role: Prominent human rights barrister who led the appeal in the spousal visa case

entities.name: Equal Opportunities Commission
entities.role: Hong Kong commission whose chairman urged a step-by-step approach to LGBT rights

entities.name: Court of Final Appeal
entities.role: Hong Kong's highest court, which ruled on spousal visas in 2018 and on spousal tax and benefits in 2019

entities.name: Inland Revenue Department
entities.role: Tax authority that was found to have unlawfully discriminated against a same-sex couple and then allowed joint tax returns for same-sex married couples

entities.name: Catholic Diocese of Hong Kong
entities.role: Group whose bid to join the civil partnerships litigation was rejected by a judge in April 2019

entities.name: Crimes Ordinance (Cap. 200)
entities.role: Law containing the provisions on homosexual offences and unequal age of consent

entities.name: Bill of Rights Ordinance
entities.role: Hong Kong law under which the unequal age of consent was found unconstitutional and sexual orientation discrimination is protected
